mhc_motif_atlas_faq.title: Frequently Asked Questions
mhc_motif_atlas_faq.text:
Home
Class I Alleles
Class II Alleles
Tools
F.A.Q.
MHC Motif Atlas: F.A.Q.
What are MHC molecules?
MHC molecules are responsible for the presentation on the cell surface of peptides recognized by T cells. MHC stands for Major Histocompatibility Complex. Two main classes of MHC molecules exist. MHC-I, also called Class I Human Leukocyte Antigen (HLA-I) in human, present intracellular peptides for recognition by CD8+ T cells. In human, HLA-I are encoded by 5 genes (HLA-A/B/C/E/G). HLA-A/B/C genes are expressed in most cell types, while HLA-E and HLA-G are only expressed in specialized cell types. MHC-I molecules form heterodimers with B2M. MHC-II present mainly extracellular peptides coming from phagocytosis or endocytosis for recognition by CD4+ T cells. MHC-II are expressed primarily in antigen presenting cells (e.g., B cells or dendritic cells). In human, MHC-II genes are encoded by 9 genes (HLA-DRA1/B1/B3/B4/B5, DPA1/B1 and DQA1/B1). Within each set of genes, MHC-II form heterodimers with an alpha chain and the beta chain (e.g., HLA-DPA1 – HLA-DPB1). MHC genes are the most polymorphic genes in the human genome and tens of thousands of different alleles have been observed in the human population. MHC molecules are found in all jawed vertebrate species.
How should I interpret the nomenclature of MHC molecules?
Due to the huge polymorphism of MHC molecules, a specific nomenclature has been established. In human, MHC are called HLA and the different alleles are designated with names like “HLA-A*01:01:01:01”. The part before the asterix refers to the gene (e.g., HLA-A or HLA-DRB1). The second part (between ‘*’ and ‘:’) refers to the main classes of MHC alleles. The third part represents polymorphisms within the main classes of MHC alleles. The fourth part represents polymorphism at the DNA level that does not change the amino acid sequence. The last part represents polymorphism in intronic regions. When dealing with proteins, the last two parts are omitted and HLA names like HLA-A*01:01 provide a unique identifier for each allele. For simplicity, the 'HLA-' can also be omitted. In mouse, MHC-I alleles start with 'H2-D/K/L' (e.g., H2-Kb) and MHC-II alleles with H2-A/E (e.g., H2-Aa-f).
What does a motif represent?
A motif is a visualization of the main sequence patterns within a group of peptides (e.g., 9-mer peptides binding to a MHC-I allele). At each position, the frequency (f_a) of each amino acid (a) is computed. These frequencies are then renormalized by the background amino acid frequencies (from the human proteome), and normalized again to 1 (i.e., p_a = raw frequency normalized by the background frequency and further normalized to 1). The height of each letter is proportional to these normalized amino acid frequencies. The total height of the letters at a given position represents the information content :

The colors of the amino acid represents their main biochemical properties: black for hydrophobic (A,F,I,L,M,P,V,W), green for polar (C,G,N,Q,S,T,Y), blue for positively charged (H,K,R), red for negatively charged (D,E). In addition, phosphorylated residues (S,T,Y) are shown in purple. All motifs shown in the MHC Motif Atlas were visualized with ggseqlogo (Wagih, Bioinformatics 2017). Motifs are very useful to rapidly grasp the main properties of a set of peptides like the ligands of a MHC molecules. Motifs are also referred to as 'sequence logos'.
What are the differences between MHC-I and MHC-II motifs?
MHC-I molecules accommodate peptides of different lengths (typically 8-14) with the main anchor residues at the second and last positions. Longer (>9) peptides generally bulge out from the binding site (see exceptions discussed in Guillaume et al. PNAS 2018). For this reason different motifs are needed to represent the properties of peptides of different lengths. MHC-II molecules bind peptides of length 12 to 21 but with a conserved 9-mer binding core and flanking residues extending on both sides of the core. Therefore the motifs of MHC-II molecules do not change across different lengths of the ligands.
What does “Peptide Length Distribution” represent?
For MHC-I alleles, the distribution of the lengths of the peptides changes substantially across alleles (e.g., HLA-A*01:01 has many long ligands, while HLA-C alleles are often much more restricted to 9-mers). This is why we show the Peptide Length Distribution for each allele. Similarly for MHC-II alleles, the peptide length distribution is shown for each allele.
What does “Multiple specificities” stand for?
For several alleles, a simple motif is too limited to describe of the binding specificity, because different classes of peptides can bind to the same allele. These different classes of peptides can represent different binding modes (e.g., C-terminal extensions in 10-mers of HLA-A*68:01 (Guillaume et al. PNAS 2018)) or different combinations of amino acids (e.g., mutually exclusive positively charged residues in HLA-B*07:02 (Bassani-Sternberg and Gfeller, 2016) or HLA-DRB1*08:01 (Racle et al. 2022)). Multiple motifs are useful to capture these different classes of peptides.
What does ‘Phosphorylated ligands’ mean?
MHC ligands are not restricted to the 20 natural amino acids, but can also display peptides containing post-translational modifications (PTMs). Among all PTMs in MHC-I ligands, phosphorylation is the one with the largest number of known peptides (Solleder et al. MCP 2020). Reliable motifs for MHC-I phosphorylated ligands could be defined and are displayed in the MHCMotifAtlas. The phosphorylated residues (S, T or Y) are shown in purple in those motifs.
What are the motifs referred to as 'Ligands'?
Amino acid frequencies in MHC ligands coming from MHC peptidomics data are strongly influenced by the amino acid frequency in the human proteome. A correct description of the MHC binding specificity needs to account for this bias by renormalizing the amino acid frequencies computed in the raw ligands. The motifs shown by default in the MHC Motif Atlas include this renormalization. For MHC alleles with known ligands, we also provide the option to visualize the motifs representing the raw ligands, without any correction for the amino acid background frequencies in the human proteome (i.e., based on f_a and not p_a values). As expected, rare amino acids in the human proteome, like M, are smaller in the motifs describing the raw ligands compared to those including renormalization by the amino acid frequencies in the human proteome that are shown by default.
What does binding core offset mean?
For MHC-II ligands, the binding is characterized by a core region of 9-amino acids (exception in one MHC-II allele in chicken with a 10-mer core) responsible for the interactions with the MHC-II binding site and flanking residues on both sides of the core. Analysis of MHC-II ligands indicate that the core is preferentially positioned at specific positions, with a preference for one residue to the right of the middle of the peptide. This can be quantified by computing the offset of the binding core from the middle of the peptide. An offset of 0 means that the core is found in the middle of a peptide with an odd length, and is not defined for peptides with an even length. An offset of 1 means that the core is shifted by one residue from the middle of the peptide towards the C-terminus (see discussion in Racle et al. Nature Biotech 2019 for the differences between peptides with odd and even numbers of residues). The fact that binding core offset shows preferences for values around 1 represents another component of the specificity of MHC-II molecules that is useful to improve predictions of MHC-II ligands.
What are N- and C-terminal motifs for MHC-II ligands
Beyond the MHC-II motifs which determine the amino acid preferences within the binding core, MHC-II ligands show specificity in their N- and C-termini. This specificity reflects the influence of the class II antigen processing pathway (e.g., cleavage, chaperone,...). The signal is especially visible at the first three and last three residues, with a preference for proline at the second position from the N-terminus.
Why don’t HLA-DR alleles include information about the HLA-DRA1 gene?
HLA-DRA1 is the only conserved, non-polymorphic HLA gene in human. As such all HLA-DRB1/3/4/5 alleles always form heterodimer with the same HLA-DRA1*01:01 allele, and therefore this information is omitted from the allele name. Reversely, HLA-DP and HLA-DQ form dimers, and the complexes are designated with the full name (HLA-DPA1*01:03 - HLA*DPB1*02:01).
Who Developed the MHC Motif Atlas?
The MHC Motif Atlas has been developed by the Gfeller Lab at the Department of Oncology and Ludwig Institute for Cancer Research at the University of Lausanne, also affiliated to the Swiss Institute of Bioinformatics.
Can I ask specific questions or give feedback?
You can contact David Gfeller by email.
How should I cite the MHC Motif Atlas?
If you use data from the MHC Motif Atlas in some of your publications, you should cite Tadros et al. NAR 2022.

Dataset used for retraining the IEDB class I binding prediction tools.
Description of the dataset: The dataset is largely identical to that of Kim et al (2014), described above, but includes additional data that was not publicly available at the time.
Date of the dataset generation: 2013
Details on the dataset generation: The dataset was compiled from three sources: the IEDB, the Sette lab, and the Buus lab. If a peptide/allele combination had more than 1 measurement among the three sources, its geometric mean was taken.
Data format: Compressed text file containing binding data.
Dataset availability: binding_data_2013.zip
Dataset used for training and testing of the NetMHCpan-4.1 method
Dataset availability: https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/suppl/immunology/NAR_NetMHCpan_NetMHCIIpan/
Dataset used for training and testing of the NetMHCpan-4.0 method
Description of the dataset: The training binding data are partitioned in 5 files to be used for cross-validation. For instance do the f000_ba and f000_el files contain the binding affinity and eluted ligand training data, and the c000_ba and c000_el files the binding affinity and eluted ligand test data for the first cross-validation partitioning. It is critical that this data partitioning is maintained.
Note that the BA data - binding affinity - are identical to the ones used for training of NetMHC-4.0 and NetMHCpan-3.0.
Dataset availability: https://services.healthtech.dtu.dk/immunology/NetMHCpan-4.0/
